standard.title: Commemoration and the Anzac Legend
standard.description: the commemoration of the First World War, including different historical interpretations and debates about the nature and significance of the Anzac legend and the war
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the causes, key events, and effects of WWI on Australian society (AC9HH9K08–K11). They have examined the wartime experience of Australian soldiers and the home front. This descriptor asks them to examine how the war is remembered and interpreted — moving from historical events to historiography and collective memory.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the commemoration of WWI, examine the Anzac legend and its interpretations, and evaluate the significance of the war including debates about post-war treaties.

nodes.label: The Anzac legend and its ideals
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the ideals associated with the Anzac tradition and explain how and why the First World War is commemorated in Australian society.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the key ideals of the Anzac tradition and explain one way WWI is commemorated in Australia.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the ideals associated with the Anzac tradition — mateship, courage, endurance, larrikinism, improvisation under fire; explain how and why WWI is commemorated (Anzac Day, memorials, the Australian War Memorial, dawn services); explain why Gallipoli became the founding moment of the legend despite being a military failure.
wider: Examine how Anzac commemorations have changed over time — from private grief in the 1920s, through Cold War patriotism, to the 'Anzac revival' of the 1990s-2000s — assessing what social and political conditions produced each shift in how the war is commemorated
Investigate how First Nations Australian soldiers have been included or excluded from Anzac commemoration over time — and examine recent efforts to recognise their service within the Anzac tradition
Compare Australian Anzac commemoration with how New Zealand commemorates WWI — examining both the shared elements and the different national emphases

response_modes.reason: The Anzac legend must be examined as a cultural construction, not simply a historical record — widening to include how commemoration has changed over time and who it has included or excluded makes this explicit.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Anzac legend's construction, evolution, and contestation is one of the richest sites for historical thinking in the Australian curriculum — it directly addresses how collective memory is made, maintained, revised, and contested, which is a transferable analytical skill.
success_criteria: Describes the key ideals of the Anzac tradition with specific examples of how they are expressed in commemoration
Explains why Gallipoli, as a military defeat, became the founding event of the Anzac legend

nodes.label: Historical interpretations of the Anzac legend
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss similarities and differences in historians' views of the Anzac legend over time and distinguish between commemoration and glorification of war.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different historical interpretations of the Anzac legend and explain how they differ.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss similarities and differences in historians' views of the Anzac legend over time; identify key interpretive debates (Was Gallipoli a military blunder? Is the Anzac legend myth or history? Does commemoration glorify war?); identify differences between commemoration (honouring sacrifice) and glorification (celebrating war); examine how the Anzac legend has been used for different ideological purposes.
wider: Examine the 'history wars' about Australian WWI history — exploring the debate between nationalist historians (e.g. those emphasising Anzac heroism) and critical historians (e.g. those examining the myth-making) — assessing what is at stake in these historiographical debates
Investigate how the Anzac legend has been used in government communication and media in the 21st century and critically assess whether this represents commemoration or glorification

Compare how different nations that fought at Gallipoli commemorate the same campaign — examining Turkish, New Zealand, and Australian commemorations to assess how the same event produces different national narratives

response_modes.reason: The commemoration/glorification distinction requires explicit reasoning — students need a clear definition and the opportunity to apply it to real examples before they can use it as an analytical tool.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two different historical interpretations of the Anzac legend and explains how they differ
Distinguishes between commemoration and glorification of war with at least one example

nodes.label: Post-war treaties and their contested fairness
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the fairness of post-war treaties on defeated powers, including the Treaty of Versailles on Germany.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles and explain one argument for or against its fairness.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles — war guilt clause, reparations, territorial losses, military restrictions; evaluate arguments for and against its fairness on Germany; consider different perspectives on the treaty (Allied leaders, German government, German people, later historians); connect the treaty's terms to the political conditions it created.
wider: Evaluate the Treaty of Versailles from multiple contemporary perspectives — the Allied leaders (Clemenceau, Wilson, Lloyd George) had different priorities — and assess how these competing interests shaped the final terms

Examine the argument that the Treaty of Versailles sowed the conditions for WWII — and critically assess whether this is an inevitable historical connection or a retrospective reading shaped by knowing what came next

Compare the Treaty of Versailles with the treatment of Allied-aligned nations after WWI (e.g. the treatment of newly created states in Eastern Europe) to assess whether the peace settlement was fair or punitive overall

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the WWI depth study by connecting the war's ending (AC9HH9K10) with its long-term consequences — the treaty conditions. It is also the site of evaluation, the highest-demand skill in the descriptor set.

success_criteria: Describes at least three major terms of the Treaty of Versailles
Evaluates at least one argument for and one argument against the treaty's fairness, drawing on historical evidence
